messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Parallel chains
parts:
Hi folks,

It occurs to me that the computation of multiple chains is an
embarrassingly parallel problem (at least, according to my beginner's
understanding of MCMC). Has any thought been put into parallelizing
chain computation in stan for systems with more than one core (i.e.
most modern systems)? I had a try at using the doMC interface to
parallelism in R for unix machines (I'm on Mac OS X) and posted the
code here:

https://gist.github.com/3861998

On my machine (1.8GHz Core i7), I get about 2x speedup using the
parallel approach. Not the full 4x speedup I might have naively
expected from my 4-core machine, but still a worthwhile improvement.
(Of course, the example is on the order of seconds in duration, so
"worthwhile" is debatable; I'll run some more computationally
intensive examples overnight to see how this scales.) Possibly deeper
integration of parallelism in stan/rstan might eliminate redundancies
and/or overhead to achieve further improvements?

I also notice that it appears that the "verbose=FALSE" argument to
stan() doesn't actually do anything...

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel chains
parts:
On Wednesday, October 10, 2012 2:06:08 AM UTC-4, Robert Long wrote:
I am very interested in the other experts reply on this as I am now
beginning to learn stan and have a huge interest in parallelisation.

I will get a new PC for my PhD next week and intend to install linux as
a dual-boot so I will definitely try your doMC code out.

We have talked about it. Implementing parallel chains in stan() via the parallel library or the doMC library would not be too difficult on Linux or a Mac because in those cases the R process is simply forked. But that route is not available on Windows. The parallel engines that do work on Windows start entirely new R processes, which is a challenge for rstan (or anything that relies on the inline package) because the executable generated by stan() somehow needs to be dynamically loaded into these new R processes.

I'm also interested in the possibility of using the CUDA architecture:
my GPU has 96 cores with 1GB shared RAM : does anyone have any thoughts
on this ?

There have been a variety of efforts to get R working with GPUs; see for example

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/OpenCL/index.html

But Stan has only been tested on Intel CPUs so far.

Ben

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel chains
parts:
If you are running from the command line, Bob has already exposed an option to shift the seed, if generated by current time (default; millisecond resolution if boost's library supports it for the OS).

I believe the option is called "chain_id". If you want to run multiple Stan processes at once, just assign different chain ids. 


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel chains
parts:
Related: this post
(http://darrenjw.wordpress.com/2010/12/14/getting-started-with-parallel-mcmc/)
has discussion of running MCMC in parallel, including the simple
parallel chains approach, but interestingly also an approach for
parallelizing individual chains (on which there is apparently more
detail in the draft chapter linked in the post). Given the
warmup-waste of the multiple chains approach, within-chain parallelism
would be exciting to see implemented, especially using OpenCL to
access the huge number of cores available on some GPUs.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel chains
parts:
Chad Scherer's Passage sampler does within-chain
parallelism in Gibbs sampling by figuring out
independent blocks. (It also compiles to C++.)
HMC's a little trickier here -- we'd need to figure
out how to parallelize our log probability calcs.

But Stan is very much like a general-purpose
imperative program in its implementation. It is
strongly typed like Fortran, so there are some things
with loops we could probably do soundly.

We're going to start with simple parallel chains.
We just discussed this in our meeting yesterday and
think we can roll out for Linux/Mac through R pretty
easily, but not so much on Windows.

I'm not so clear on how we could parallelize a single chain
in Stan. Even if we had a parallel matrix lib for
some operations, there's an issue with the re-entrancy
of our auto-dif across threads (we use thread local
to synch if necessary, and that won't work if we
add multiple cores per thread).

Parallelizing with things like GPUs in R doesn't
help. First, GPUs are a pain and only work on
32-bit vectorized ops, which is just not how Stan's
layed out. Second, speeding up R doesn't help because
Stan's written in C++. Within epsilon, all the
time is spent in compiling the Stan program and
executing the C++.

- Bob

messages.author: ba46e0c634632e6f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel chains
parts: I am also interested in parallelization options, and having the ability to easily run chains in parallel when calling rstan makes the most sense to me. GPU acceleration may work well for some large problems, but it is likely to be hard to generalize for every problem (and might not make sense in a lot of cases). And as Bob mentioned, this would have to be implemented inside of the C++ somewhere.
